name: Redis Inc. (formerly Garantia Data, then Redis Labs)
origin_detail: Redis itself was created by Salvatore Sanfilippo (antirez) in 2009 to scale his LLOOGG analytics service, sponsored by VMware (2010-13) and Pivotal (2013-15). The company was founded in Israel in 2011 as Garantia Data by Ofer Bengal and Yiftach Shoolman to sell Redis-based database services; it renamed itself Redis Labs in 2014, hired antirez in July 2015 to become the project's official sponsor, and became 'Redis' in August 2021. Israeli-founded, California-based (offices in San Francisco, Austin, London, Tel Aviv per CB Insights).
openness_notes: The company never owned a fully open product line: core Redis was BSD-3-Clause, while Redis Enterprise was proprietary and its modules moved from AGPL to Apache+Commons Clause (2018) to RSAL (2019). From Redis 7.4 (March 2024) the core went to RSALv2/SSPLv1 (level 1). Redis 8 (May 2025) added AGPLv3 as an option, restoring an OSI licence for the core alongside proprietary Redis Enterprise/Cloud (level 2).

license_history.note: Core stayed BSD through Redis 7.2.x, including during the 2018-19 module changes.
RediSearch, RedisGraph, ReJSON, ReBloom, Redis-ML moved from AGPL; aimed at cloud managed services.

license_history.license: AGPLv3 or RSALv2 or SSPLv1 (core, from Redis 8)

relicensing_events.outcome_note: Core unaffected; criticism from the open-source community.

relicensing_events.fork: Valkey (from Redis 7.2.4, BSD-3-Clause), announced 2024-03-28 under the Linux Foundation
relicensing_events.fork_backer: AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle, Ericsson, Snap (Linux Foundation governance)
relicensing_events.outcome_note: AWS now recommends Valkey as the default ElastiCache engine and shipped Valkey 9.0 (May 2026) and 9.1 (June 2026). Redis's CEO said SSPL mainly 'applies to Amazon and Google'.
Followed antirez's return to Redis in November 2024. Commentators said the damage looked long-lasting: 'Once you've migrated to a fork, there's no business case to migrate back'.

risk_events: 2018-2019: Module relicensing (Commons Clause, then RSAL) drew criticism
2024-03: Core relicensed to RSALv2/SSPLv1; Linux Foundation fork Valkey launched within 8 days, backed by AWS, Google and Oracle
2026: AWS positions Valkey as the recommended ElastiCache engine (Valkey 9.0 May 2026, 9.1 June 2026)
2025-05: Partial reversal to AGPLv3 with Redis 8
No IPO as of Jul 2026 per trackers; secondary-market estimates (~$1.3B, QuantLogix) sit below the 2021 $2B round
robustness: Single-vendor control of the Redis trademark and code; the BSD-licensed lineage now lives on in Valkey under neutral Linux Foundation governance with hyperscaler backing, so users have an exit. The company reported passing $300M ARR in January 2026 with 50+ customers above $1M a year, and is buying into AI/streaming (Decodable, announced 2025-09-04). Private, last priced in 2021.
physical_science_relevance: Commonly used as a cache, queue and pub/sub broker in lab automation and data pipelines.
openness_effect_assessment: The BSD licence made Redis ubiquitous, which is why a company that did not create it could build a business around it. Closing the core in 2024 produced the fastest fork in this group (Valkey, within 8 days) with AWS, Google and Oracle behind it, and AWS has since steered its large ElastiCache base to Valkey. Redis's AGPL return in 2025 restored an OSI licence but not the lost cloud channel.
key_takeaway: Redis shows the limits of relicensing when the hyperscalers are your biggest distribution channel: the moment the core closed, they forked it into a neutral foundation and made the fork their default. Redis Inc. still grew past $300M ARR, but it has not IPO'd and secondary markets value it below its 2021 $2B round. The reversal to AGPL after antirez returned suggests the company concluded that the open-source label mattered more for developer adoption than the licence protection did.
